details:
**"A spectre is haunting Europe"**
The famous opening line of the Manifesto: "A spectre is haunting Europe – the spectre of communism." The preamble says all the powers of old Europe, including the Pope, the Tsar, Metternich, Guizot, French Radicals, and German police spies, have entered into a "holy alliance to exorcise" this spectre.

**"The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles"**
The opening sentence of Section I, "Bourgeois and Proletarians," which states the work's central thesis. It traces history through oppressor and oppressed classes, such as freeman and slave or lord and serf, down to the modern struggle between the bourgeoisie (owners of the means of production) and the proletariat (wage workers).

**Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, 1848**
The Manifesto was written by Marx and Engels for the Communist League and published in London in February 1848, just as revolutions broke out across Europe. It is a short pamphlet promoting communism as the outcome of a proletarian revolution against capitalism.

**Ten-point program**
The list of ten measures at the end of Section II, which the authors say will be applicable in most advanced countries. It includes a heavy progressive income tax, abolition of the right of inheritance, centralization of credit in a state bank, establishment of industrial armies (especially for agriculture), and free education for all children in public schools.

**"Workers of the world, unite!"**
The closing slogan of the Manifesto, more literally "Proletarians of all countries, unite!" It follows the line "The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win."

**Specters of Marx and "hauntology"**
Jacques Derrida's 1993 book Specters of Marx, whose title alludes to the Manifesto's opening "spectre." In it Derrida coined "hauntology," a pun on "ontology," for the way the ideas and themes of the past keep returning to haunt the present.

**"Abolition of private property"**
The Manifesto says the theory of the communists can be summed up in this single sentence. It specifies that it means the abolition of bourgeois property, used to exploit others' labor, rather than personal belongings.

**Abolition of the family and religion**
In Section II the authors answer objections that communists want to abolish the family, pleading guilty to wanting "to stop the exploitation of children by their parents." They also dismiss objections from religion and morality, which they see as reflecting ruling-class interests.

**The bourgeoisie as its own "grave-diggers"**
At the end of Section I, the Manifesto argues that by building modern industry and gathering workers together in factories, the bourgeoisie creates the proletariat that will overthrow it. "What the bourgeoisie therefore produces, above all, are its own grave-diggers."

**"All that is solid melts into air"**
A famous phrase from Section I describing how capitalism constantly revolutionizes production and dissolves traditional social relations, so that man is finally compelled to face "his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind." Marshall Berman used it as the title of his 1982 book on modernity.

**"Idiocy of rural life"**
The Manifesto praises the bourgeoisie for rescuing much of the population from the "idiocy of rural life." Eric Hobsbawm, in his introduction to the Verso edition, noted that the original sense is closer to the "isolation" of rural life, from the Greek idiotes, a private person cut off from public affairs.

**Discovery of America and rounding of the Cape**
Section I explains that the discovery of America and the rounding of the Cape of Good Hope opened new markets and trade. This fueled the rise of the bourgeoisie and the decline of feudal society.

**Proudhon's Philosophy of Poverty**
In Section III, which critiques other socialist writings, the Manifesto names Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's Philosophy of Poverty as an example of "Conservative, or Bourgeois, Socialism." It says economists, philanthropists, and humanitarians belong to this camp, which seeks to fix social problems while keeping bourgeois society intact.

**Section IV and other opposition parties**
The short final section describes where communists stand in relation to various opposition parties. It mentions supporting the Social-Democrats in France and the Radicals in Switzerland, and it ends with the call for workers to unite.

**"The free development of each is the condition for the free development of all"**
The Manifesto's description, at the end of Section II, of the association that will replace class-divided bourgeois society once class distinctions disappear.
